newsitem.title: BELGIUM: European film makers seek film fund, EU hesitates.
newsitem.headline: European film makers seek film fund, EU hesitates.

text.p: Europe's film makers on Monday urged the European Union to delay no further the establishment of a fund to help them, saying it was essential to breathe new life into an ailing but potentially job-creating industry.
But the bloc's culture ministers failed to tie up plans for the fund, delaying agreement until at least the early months of next year.

The European Film Companies Alliance (EFCA) -- grouping major film makers including PolyGram, Bertelsmann and Rank, said the future of Europe's film industry -- currently running a $5 billion trade deficit with the United States -- was at stake.

The European Commission has urged EU governments to set up a 90 million European currency unit ($108 million) loan guarantee fund, saying it would last 17 years and generate enough capital to finance 415 films and 215 television productions.
The fund -- which would be managed by the European Investment Fund -- would encourage financial institutions to invest in European film production by guaranteeing a proportion of the loans they make.
"European audiences are more and more watching American films," Stewart Till, president of PolyGram Filmed Entertainment, told a news conference.

"Yet American audiences are not returning that favour. They are with very few exceptions ignoring European films. What is wanting is not talent...nor is it a question of production...If there's one reason for the problem, EFCA would argue that it's a question of funding."
The culture ministers met a month after the European Parliament dropped demands for EU action to restrict Hollywood imports.

The film makers, who say they prefer the idea of a guarantee fund to protection against U.S. imports, say Europe's audiovisual sector, if properly funded, could help create two million jobs over the next 10 years.
To overcome German-led resistance, Ireland, which holds the EU's presidency, proposed slashing the planned budget by a third to 60 million Ecus ($72 million).

While diplomats said that Germany came around to the idea, it was still unclear how funds would be distributed between bigger film makers, able to make commercially viable films, and smaller and medium-sized groups which had lobbied strongly for quotas on Hollywood films.

Hollywood is able to cover production costs in its enormous monolingual domestic market and then sell its films and television programmes in Europe at a tenth of the price it would cost Europeans to make something similar, industry sources say.

The diversity of languages makes distribution difficult in the 15-nation EU market. As a result, eight out of 10 films shown in the cinema and six out of 10 shown on television in Europe are from the United States.
